Chapter 3: Encounters and Misunderstandings—Navigating Cultural Differences
Living in a new place isn’t just about getting used to the landscape or the weather. It’s about figuring out how to build relationships with people whose customs and beliefs often feel completely different from your own.
In Thika, the family quickly finds themselves right at the crossroads of cultures. There’s curiosity on both sides, but there’s also plenty of confusion. Sometimes, misunderstandings seem almost inevitable.
The local people have their own traditions and ways of life. They’re the family’s neighbors, and often their collaborators, too. The family relies on them for so much—labor, guidance, even a sense of belonging. But those relationships are rarely simple. Communication is a challenge all on its own. With language barriers, it’s easy for confusion to slip in, and sometimes, people get offended without anyone meaning to. The father, who’s used to giving instructions and seeing things done his way, often struggles to understand what really matters to his workers. The mother, who tries hard to pay attention to subtle differences, does her best to build bridges, but even her kindest efforts can sometimes be met with confusion—or even resistance.
For their child, though, these moments are a source of endless fascination. Daily life is filled with new sights and sounds: songs drifting through the air while people work, rituals that mark the start and end of the day, stories shared around a meal. There’s something magical about watching women carry water so gracefully, or hearing laughter ripple through a group during lunch. The child’s natural openness makes it easier to make friends—even when adults might hesitate—and those friendships offer a peek into a world that feels both strange and welcoming.
Of course, not every encounter goes smoothly. Sometimes, what’s meant as a friendly gesture gets misunderstood, or a simple request leaves everyone scratching their heads. The family learns, sometimes the hard way, that making assumptions can be risky. Patience becomes their greatest ally. Over time, though, they start to appreciate how complex the local culture really is—and realize that their own way of doing things isn’t always the best, or even the only, way.
One of the most surprising parts of life in Thika is how humor and empathy become lifelines. When things get tense, a little laughter can go a long way. It’s amazing how a shared joke—even one that starts because of a misunderstanding—can bring people together. The family learns to laugh at themselves, to accept that mistakes will happen, and to greet each new experience with a bit of humility.
The child, especially, becomes quite skilled at moving between cultures. With fewer preconceived ideas, it’s easier to form real connections with friends whose lives are shaped by traditions stretching back generations. These friendships aren’t always simple, but they open up a world rich with meaning and possibility.
As the family becomes more woven into the community, something shifts. They begin to see the land through new eyes. The local people’s deep knowledge—the way they understand the seasons, the animals, the plants—turns out to be invaluable. The family comes to respect this wisdom, learning that thriving in Thika isn’t just about hard work; it’s about building strong, respectful relationships.
Most of the time, people don’t realize just how much there is to gain by embracing difference. In Thika, the family discovers that cultural encounters aren’t just about conflict—they’re about growth. Every misunderstanding brings a chance to learn. Every new friendship becomes an opportunity to change and expand.
And, as the days pass, those old lines between “us” and “them” start to fade—replaced by a sense of shared humanity that’s richer and deeper than the family ever expected.
